title: Diffraction and Polarization
notes: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave when it passes an edge or a narrow opening. It is noticeable when the opening is comparable with the wavelength.
A single slit of width a has a bright central band. The first dark band on each side satisfies sinθ = λ / a. A smaller a means a larger angle, so a narrower slit makes a wider pattern.
The central band is twice as wide as the side bands. Most of the light is in that centre. This is not the equal spacing of Young's two-slit fringes.
A diffraction grating has many slits. The principal maxima are sharp and satisfy d sinθ = m λ, and they are used to measure wavelength.
Polarisation is included here as the other wave property. Unpolarised light through one Polaroid emerges plane polarised at about half the intensity. A second Polaroid at angle θ then follows Malus.
This exercise is the single-slit angle. Brewster's angle was the other page, so the numbers are not repeated.
confusion: ❌ 'Diffraction and interference are the same thing.' ✅ Diffraction is bending of waves around obstacles/slits; interference is superposition of waves from *two or more coherent sources*.
❌ 'Polarization applies to all waves.' ✅ Only *transverse* waves can be polarized; longitudinal waves (e.g., sound) cannot.
❌ 'A single slit produces no diffraction pattern.' ✅ A single slit produces a *diffraction* pattern with a central bright maximum and weaker side fringes.
Single-slit fringes are not equally spaced like Young's.
A narrower slit gives a wider diffraction pattern.
The centre of a single slit is bright.
Half intensity is the first Polaroid on unpolarised light, before Malus.
